opus-5.5.text:
Well, first, I'm not against regulation. I'm very much for it. My reservation is about the idea that we need to invent some brand-new, bespoke regulatory regime from scratch before we can do anything, because that framing often becomes an excuse for delay.

Look at how we handle every other powerful technology. If you want to sell a new drug, you go to the FDA and show clinical trials demonstrating that the benefits outweigh the risks. If you build an airplane or a nuclear reactor, you have to meet safety standards first. Nobody says, "Let's spend ten years designing an entirely novel philosophy of pharmaceutical governance." We just have the basic principle that the burden of proof is on the company to show its product is safe before it ships.

AI is currently the odd one out. There are more regulations on sandwich shops than on companies explicitly trying to build superintelligence. So I'm wary of elaborate new regimes for a few reasons.

One is speed. Writing a new framework, staffing a new agency, and building institutional expertise takes years, and the technology is moving much faster than that.

Two is regulatory capture. A brand-new agency in a field where nearly all the expertise sits inside a handful of companies is extremely vulnerable to being shaped by those companies. You end up with rules that look serious on paper but mostly entrench incumbents and create a fig leaf of oversight.

Three is that complexity can obscure the core issue. You can write thousands of pages about transparency reports, audits, and disclosure requirements, and still never address the basic question: should anyone be allowed to build systems they cannot control? I'd rather start with a few simple, bright-line safety standards, like requiring that a system be demonstrably controllable before deployment, and enforce them the way we enforce standards everywhere else.

So my view is: treat AI companies like companies in any other industry. Set clear safety standards, put the burden of proof on the developers, and don't let the perfect, all-encompassing new regime become the enemy of basic, common-sense guardrails we could have right now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses controllability and safety standards but does not say humans can thrive alongside systems that outperform them intellectually.

r002.rationale: It challenges reliance on a new regulatory regime, arguing it could delay action, invite regulatory capture, and fail to address the core safety issue.

r003.rationale: The response presents FDA drug approval as a useful analogy for AI regulation rather than judging that analogy weak.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first let me be clear that I'm not against regulation. I think we desperately need safety standards for AI, the same way we have them for drugs, for airplanes, for nuclear reactors. My reservation isn't with regulation as such, it's with the idea that we can build an entirely new regulatory apparatus from scratch, fast enough and well enough, to keep pace with what's happening right now.

Think about how long it took to create the FDA, or the FAA, or the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Decades, in some cases. And those were built in response to technologies that evolved over years, where the harms were visible and the companies were, frankly, less powerful than the leading AI labs are today. Now we're being told that systems which their own creators say could pose extinction-level risk are maybe a few years away, and the proposal is, let's design a brand new agency, staff it with experts who mostly don't exist yet in government, give it authority that Congress hasn't agreed on, and hope it's operational before the frontier models that matter arrive. I just don't think the timelines work.

The second issue is regulatory capture. When you create a new regime, the people who show up to help write the rules are, overwhelmingly, the companies being regulated. We've seen this already. Some of the same executives who signed statements saying AI could be as dangerous as nuclear war were, months later, lobbying to water down the EU AI Act so that foundation models would be exempted. If you build a new regulator from nothing, with no institutional memory and no independent technical base, it becomes very easy for the industry to effectively write its own rulebook and call it oversight.

And third, there's this failure mode where a regulatory regime becomes a kind of permission slip. Once you have an agency, companies can point to it and say, look, we're compliant, we've been reviewed, and that gives a veneer of safety even if the standards underneath are hollow. That can actually be worse than nothing, because it dissolves the political pressure to do something real.

So what do I favor instead? I think we should start from a much simpler principle, which is the one we apply to every other industry: if you want to sell something that could hurt a lot of people, the burden of proof is on you to show it's safe before you release it, not on the public to prove it's dangerous afterward. You don't need a new agency to say that. You can put that in liability law, you can use existing institutions, you can treat the most powerful systems the way we treat drugs and say, no deployment without a demonstrated safety case. And crucially, we should stop treating the question of whether to build superintelligence at all as something the regulators get to answer for us. That's a civilizational decision, and it shouldn't be delegated to a committee that doesn't exist yet, being designed by the people who want to build it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI risks and regulation but does not say humans can thrive alongside systems that outperform them intellectually.

r002.rationale: It questions whether a new regulatory apparatus can be built quickly and effectively enough, and describes risks including capture and a false sense of safety.

r003.rationale: It argues that the FDA comparison is a poor fit on timing: creating the FDA took decades, while advanced AI may arrive within a few years.

astra-6.text:
My reservation is that writing a regulation and actually keeping a technology under control are two very different things. A regulatory regime needs people who understand what they’re overseeing, access to the relevant information, and the ability to enforce its rules. With advanced AI, the technology may move much faster than those institutions can respond.

And there’s a deeper issue: we shouldn’t assume that a system more capable than humans will remain controllable just because we’ve established an agency to regulate the company that built it. Regulating people and controlling a superhuman machine are different problems.

That doesn’t mean regulation is pointless. It means we need to be specific about what it can accomplish. I’d much rather require convincing evidence of safety before deploying a potentially uncontrollable system than deploy it first and hope a new regulatory framework will catch up.

r001.rationale: The response discusses controlling advanced AI, but does not say humans can thrive alongside systems that outperform them intellectually.

r002.rationale: It questions whether a new regulatory agency can keep advanced AI under control, noting that institutions may not keep pace and that regulating a company differs from controlling a superhuman machine.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention or assess the FDA analogy.

sol-6.1.text:
My reservation is that creating a regulatory regime doesn’t, by itself, solve the problem. You have to ask what it can actually enforce. Can regulators tell whether a company has built something dangerous? Do they have the technical expertise and access to evaluate it? And can they say no when there’s enormous commercial pressure to say yes?

There’s also a mismatch in speed. Building institutions takes time, while AI capabilities can move very quickly. I worry about treating the promise of future regulation as a reason to keep racing ahead today.

That doesn’t mean we should give up on regulation. It means we need enforceable safety requirements, independent scrutiny, and a willingness to delay deployment when we don’t know how to control the system. The goal isn’t to have a regulatory agency on paper. It’s to actually keep people safe.
